opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's something deeply right about it, and it's actually a very old idea. You can trace it back to Helmholtz in the nineteenth century, who talked about perception as "unconscious inference." The basic problem is that what reaches your eyes is just this two-dimensional array of light hitting your retina, and from that impoverished information you somehow reconstruct a three-dimensional world full of objects with stable shapes and colors and positions. Graphics goes from a model of the world to an image; vision has to go backwards, from the image to the model of the world that most likely produced it. And that's a genuinely hard inference problem, because any given image is consistent with infinitely many possible worlds.

What's been exciting in the last couple of decades is that we've gotten much more precise ways of thinking about that, especially probabilistic, Bayesian models. The idea is that the visual system has something like a generative model, a model of how worlds produce images, and then it uses the data to work out which world is most probable. And a lot of the classic visual illusions turn out to make sense that way. They're not bugs; they're cases where the system is making the rational bet given what it usually encounters.

Now, where I'd add some caution, and where my work with children comes in, is that the inverse graphics picture can make it sound as if the generative model is just sitting there, fixed, and perception is a kind of passive decoding. But the really interesting question is where those models come from and how they change. Babies aren't just running inverse graphics on a fixed engine. They're actively exploring, they're experimenting, they're figuring out what the causal structure of the world is, and their models of the world are being revised all the time. Vision is in service of action and learning, not just reconstruction.

And I think that's also a useful contrast with a lot of current AI vision systems, which are very good at picking up statistical patterns in images, but don't necessarily have that rich, structured, causal model of the three-dimensional world behind them. So I'd say inverse graphics is a great description of part of what vision is doing, but the deeper and more interesting story is the learning: how a child goes from being a baby to having this extraordinarily rich model of the world that makes the inversion possible in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response explains that graphics maps a world model to an image, while vision works backward from the image to infer the likely world, using a generative model of how worlds produce images.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the great ideas in cognitive science, and it's an idea that's really deeply rooted in what I'd call the Bayesian picture of the mind. The basic thought is that what the visual system is doing is running a kind of generative model in reverse. Graphics takes a three-dimensional scene — objects, surfaces, light sources — and renders a two-dimensional image. Vision takes the two-dimensional image hitting your retina and tries to infer what three-dimensional scene would have produced it. It's inference to the best explanation, and the beautiful thing is that it makes vision look like a species of theorizing, which is exactly what I've argued children are doing when they learn about the world more generally.

So I'm very sympathetic. In some ways it's the Helmholtz idea of unconscious inference finally made precise and computational — people like Josh Tenenbaum and Tom Griffiths and others have shown that you can actually build systems that do this and that match human judgments remarkably well.

Where I'd put some pressure on it is in two places. First, the inverse graphics picture tends to assume you already have the right generative model — you know about objects and occlusion and light. The really interesting developmental question is where that model comes from in the first place, and the answer can't just be inverse graphics all the way down. Babies are learning the forward model and the inverse at the same time, and they're doing it by acting on the world, moving their heads, reaching, pushing things over, not just passively receiving images. Vision is deeply entangled with exploration.

Second, the pure inverse graphics story can make it sound as if perception has a single goal, which is to recover the true scene. But perception is in the service of what you're going to do next, and different creatures, and even the same person in different states — a two-year-old versus a focused adult — may be optimizing for very different things. The child's visual system looks less like a camera trying to get the picture right and more like a scientist doing lots of noisy, high-variance experiments. So I'd say inverse graphics is roughly right as a description of the computation, but it's incomplete as a description of the mind that's doing it.

r001.rationale: The response says vision runs a generative model in reverse, inferring the 3D scene that produced the 2D image hitting the retina.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very fruitful idea, but it depends on what you mean by it. If you mean that we have some model of how the world generates the light that reaches our eyes, and that perception works backward to figure out what’s out there, that seems like a powerful way of thinking about vision.

The interesting question for me is where that model comes from. You can build a system that does inverse graphics if you’ve already given it the right representations of objects and space. But a baby has to learn a great deal about how objects behave, and does that partly by acting on the world—reaching, moving, picking things up, seeing what happens.

So I’d want to put inverse graphics inside a broader picture of learning and exploration. We’re not just looking at an image and inferring its cause. We’re moving around in the world and doing little experiments that help us discover what the causes could be.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model of how the world generates light reaching the eyes and says perception works backward from that visual input to infer what is in the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very fruitful idea. The basic thought is that you have some model of how the world produces the images that reach your eyes, and perception involves working backward from those images to what’s out there in the world. That captures something important about how perception works, especially the fact that what we see goes beyond the information that’s immediately available at the retina.

But I think the interesting question is where those models come from. If you’re thinking about a baby, you can’t simply assume that the baby already has a sophisticated graphics program in its head. You have to explain how that structure develops through experience. And babies don’t just sit there receiving images. They move their heads, reach for things, pick things up. They’re actively doing things that help them figure out what the world is like. So I think inverse graphics is a powerful framework, but it needs to be embedded in an account of learning and action.

r001.rationale: The response describes an internal model of how the world produces images and says perception works backward from those images to infer what is in the world.
